issues.title: MinMaxStructState::emit_to(EmitTo::First(n)) subtracts row counts from a byte counter
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

Filed as a follow up to review comments in https://github.com/apache/datafusion-comet/pull/7191#discussion_r4407318204. 

 In datafusion-functions-aggregate/src/min_max/min_max_struct.rs, set_value adds get_array_memory_size() bytes to total_data_bytes for each stored struct. But emit_to(EmitTo::First(n)) subtracts s.len() for each emitted value, which is 1 for a one-row StructArray. So size() keeps counting memory for groups that were already emitted. It only resets on EmitTo::All.

Ordered aggregation emits First(n) after every batch, so the reported size grows with the number of groups seen. Reproduction: a Partial AggregateExec feeding a Final one over sorted input, with 4,096 groups of 4 KiB struct values, 64-row batches, a 2 MiB GreedyMemoryPool and the disk manager disabled. It fails with ResourcesExhausted in OrderedFinalAggregateStream. Subtracting get_array_memory_size() of the emitted values instead makes it complete.

 The code looks copied from min_max_bytes, where len() is a byte count.

issues.title: Avoid re-evaluating build keys in array_map_key_range
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

`array_map_key_range` (`datafusion/physical-plan/src/joins/hash_join/exec.rs`) takes the build batches and, under `NullEqualsNull`, evaluates the join key expressions again to check for nulls. It also sums `num_rows` over the batches.

After #26793, `build_in_memory` concatenates first and has already evaluated the keys into `left_values` before it calls `array_map_key_range`, which now always gets that one concatenated batch. For a computed key that is an array map candidate under `NullEqualsNull`, the keys are evaluated twice, and the second copy covers the whole build side rather than one input batch at a time.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Pass `&left_values[0]` (for the null count) and `num_rows` to `array_map_key_range` instead of `&[RecordBatch]`. This drops the duplicate evaluation and the row count loop, and makes the function's inputs match what it actually uses.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Leave it as is. It only matters for computed integer keys under `NullEqualsNull`, and the extra evaluation is transient.

### Additional context

Came up in review of #26793 (follows #26792).

### Willingness to contribute

I cannot contribute to this feature at this time

issues.title: PartitionedTopKExec with DENSE_RANK retains every input batch a retained row came from
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

With `datafusion.optimizer.enable_window_topn = true`, a `DENSE_RANK()` top-K query holds memory proportional to its **input**, not to the rows it retains, for every payload type (Int64 included).

`PartitionedTopKDenseRank::insert_batch` registers the whole input batch in its `RecordBatchStore`
(`self.store.register(batch.clone())`), and the batch stays there as long as any retained row references it. There
is no gather of the admitted rows and no compaction, so one surviving row keeps its whole batch alive. `ROW_NUMBER` and `RANK` avoid this through `PartitionedTopKCore`: they gather only the admitted rows and compact the store on a row ratio (#25730, #25968). `DENSE_RANK` hasn't been moved over.

### To Reproduce

In `datafusion-cli`, create 4.1M rows in which each 8192-row batch introduces 10 new partitions (same data as #26381):

    COPY (
      SELECT CAST((i / 8192) * 10 + (i % 10) AS BIGINT) AS pk,
             CAST(i AS BIGINT) AS v,
             concat(md5(CAST(i AS VARCHAR)), md5(CAST(i + 1 AS VARCHAR)),
                    md5(CAST(i + 2 AS VARCHAR)), substr(md5(CAST(i + 3 AS VARCHAR)), 1, 18)) AS s
      FROM generate_series(0, 4095999) AS t(i)
      ORDER BY i
    ) TO '/tmp/ptk.parquet' STORED AS PARQUET;

    CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE t STORED AS PARQUET LOCATION '/tmp/ptk.parquet';
    SET datafusion.execution.target_partitions = 1;
    SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_window_topn = true;
    SELECT count(*), sum(length(s)), sum(pk), sum(v), sum(rn)
    FROM (SELECT pk, v, s, dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY pk ORDER BY v) AS rn FROM t)
    WHERE rn <= 1;

The query retains 5,000 rows. Smallest passing `--memory-limit`:

| | memory limit |
|---|---|
| `dense_rank()`, `enable_window_topn = true` | **1046M** |
| `dense_rank()`, `enable_window_topn = false` (sort plan, spills) | 17M |

At the operator level, with K=1 and the same 200 batches of 8192 rows (10 survivors spread through each batch)
fed to all three operators, the stores hold:

| payload | ROW_NUMBER | RANK | DENSE_RANK | input |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Int64 | 31 KB (2,002 rows) | 31 KB (2,001 rows) | **25,600 KB (1,638,400 rows)** | 25,600 KB |
| Utf8 | 247 KB | 246 KB | **224,012 KB** | 224,012 KB |

### Expected behavior

Retained memory proportional to the retained rows (the rows of K distinct ORDER BY values per partition), as with `ROW_NUMBER` and `RANK`, and no more than the sort plan the rewrite replaces.

### Additional context

Gathering the admitted rows alone isn't enough. With survivors spread across batches the store still grows with
the input unless it is also compacted; that is why `PartitionedTopKCore` compacts at `STORE_COMPACTION_RATIO`. One difference from `RANK`: `DENSE_RANK` keeps every row of each of its K retained ORDER BY values, so an evicted value releases all of its rows at once.

issues.title: [EPIC] Improve I/O patterns for Parquet scans
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

I feel like there is no good writeup of the high level project / goals for the parquet reader / IO system that @adriangb, @Dandandan, @hhhizzz, @HippoBaro, @zhuqi-lucas @etseidl @XiangpengHao @Rich-T-kid @haohuaijin @neilconway and @mbutrovich  and others has been working on recently, so I wanted to try and write it up

Today the DataFusion Parquet scan reads an entire row group into memory in one request, decodes it, and only then fetches the next row group. This is a hard coded trade-off between I/O latency and memory that users can not change. The user visible effects are:

1. **Time to first batch** scales with row group size: on object storage the first rows of a large row group arrive only after the whole row group has been downloaded.
2. **Peak memory** per partition is at least one full row group (often 100MB+), regardless of `batch_size` or the memory pool limit, and is not reclaimable.
3. **I/O and decode do not overlap** within a partition: the fetch of row group N+1 does not start until row group N has been fully decoded.
4. **Enabling `pushdown_filters` changes the I/O pattern** to many smaller sequential requests (filter columns first, then projection columns). That can be slower on high latency stores and is one reason it is still off by default (see #20324, #24393, #24527).
5. **No way to tune for the storage system**: a local SSD or in-memory cache would benefit from more, smaller reads; a remote object store from fewer, larger reads. The only knob today is `metadata_size_hint`.

* Items 1 and 2 are tracked at the reader level in apache/arrow-rs#11234.
* Item 3 is already tracked by https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/18470

Visually, here is how the DataFusion reader read two row groups, RG1 and RG2 today:

```text
   time    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶

           ┌───────────────────────────┐                        ┌───────────────────────────┐
   I/O     │     fetch ALL of RG 1     │        ~ idle ~        │     fetch ALL of RG 2     │        ~ idle ~
           │  (one request, ~100 MB)   │                        │  (one request, ~100 MB)   │
           └───────────────────────────┘                        └───────────────────────────┘
─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
                                        ┌──────────────────────┐                             ┌───────────────────────┐
   CPU               ~ idle ~           │     decode RG 1      │          ~ idle ~           │      decode RG 2      │
                 (waiting for I/O)      │   (batch by batch)   │      (waiting for I/O)      │   (batch by batch)    │
                                        └──────────────────────┘                             └───────────────────────┘
─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
                                        ┌──────────────────────┐                             ┌───────────────────────┐
  Output             no output          │   batches of RG 1    │          no output          │    batches of RG 2    │
            (until ALL of RG 1 fetched) │       emitted        │ (until ALL of RG 2 fetched) │        emitted        │
                                        └──────────────────────┘                             └───────────────────────┘
─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
                       ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐            ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  Memory               │     RG 1 fully buffered (~100 MB)     │            │     RG 2 fully buffered (~100 MB)      │
                       │  from first byte fetched until last   │            │from first byte fetched until last batch│
                       └───────────────────────────────────────┘            └────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

However, depending on your systems IO speed and RAM budget/buffering and other factors you may want different patters.

For example, on a object store which has high throughput but low latency you probably want to start  next fetch as early as possible

```
   time    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶

           ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
   I/O     │fetch ALL of RG 1 (one large request) ││fetch ALL of RG 2, issued IMMEDIATELY │         ~ idle ~
           │    long latency, high throughput     ││  while RG 1 is still being decoded   │(or start reading next RG)
           └──────────────────────────────────────┘└──────────────────────────────────────┘
─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
                                                   ┌────────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────────┐
   CPU                     ~ idle ~                │      decode RG 1       │  short wait  │      decode RG 2       │
            (unavoidable: first request in flight) │(overlaps fetch of RG 2)│ (I/O bound)  │ (starts as soon as it  │
                                                   └────────────────────────┘              └────────────────────────┘
─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
                                                   ┌────────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────────┐
  Output                  no output                │    batches of RG 1     │              │    batches of RG 2     │
               (waiting for the first request)     │        emitted         │              │        emitted         │
                                                   └────────────────────────┘              └────────────────────────┘
─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
           ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
           │RG 1 buffered (~100 MB) from first byte until last batch decoded│
           │                                                                │
  Memory   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                                   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                                                   │ RG 2 buffered (~100 MB): overlaps RG 1, so peak = 2 row groups │
                                                   │                           (~200 MB)                            │
                                                   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

But on a LOCAL SSD, with a tiny latency per request, interleaving small fetches with decode is probably a better strategy:

```
   time    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶

           ┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐
   I/O     │fetch RG 1 ││fetch RG 1 ││fetch RG 1 ││fetch RG 1 ││fetch RG 2 ││fetch RG 2 ││fetch RG 2 │      done
           │ pages 1-2 ││ pages 3-4 ││ pages 5-6 ││ pages 7-8 ││ pages 1-2 ││ pages 3-4 ││ pages 5-6 │
           └───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘
─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
                        ┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐┌───────────┐
   CPU         wait     │decode RG 1││decode RG 1││decode RG 1││decode RG 1││decode RG 2││decode RG 2││decode RG 2│
            (1st pages) │ pages 1-2 ││ pages 3-4 ││ pages 5-6 ││ pages 7-8 ││ pages 1-2 ││ pages 3-4 ││ pages 5-6 │
                        └───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘└───────────┘
─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
                        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  Output     no output  │        batches emitted continuously: the first batch appears after a few pages,         │
                        │                               not after a whole row group                               │
                        └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
           ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  Memory   │             only the read-ahead buffer (e.g. 8 MB): the pages of the next batch or two,              │
           │                                       never a whole row group                                        │
           └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

There are many other combinations like if you have a shared cache, for example

### Describe the solution you'd like

Make the Parquet scan I/O pattern configurable rather than single hard coded reader implementation. Some ideas:

- Use the `ParquetPushDecoder` scan plan so DataFusion, not arrow-rs, decides which byte ranges to fetch and when (#26387, apache/arrow-rs#11234).
- Fetch and decode at batch (or page) granularity with bounded read-ahead, so the first batch is returned after a few MB instead of a full row group and peak memory is bounded by the read-ahead budget rather than the row group size (#24086).
- Prefetch the next row group (or next pages) while the current one is being decoded, so I/O and CPU overlap within a partition.
- Keep the one-request-per-row-group pattern as an option when `pushdown_filters` is enabled, so filter pushdown never issues more requests than the default path (#24393, #24527).
- Expose a small number of settings (for example a read-ahead budget in bytes and a request coalescing threshold) with defaults tuned for object storage, and document them in the tuning guide (#16178).
- Add tests that assert on the object store request pattern (count and size of ranges) so regressions are caught in CI, as arrow-rs does (apache/arrow-rs#7971).


### Describe alternatives you've considered

The high level idea I think we are pursuing is:

1. @adriangb / @sunchao / @zhuqi-lucas: arrow-rs lets the ParquetPushDecoder communicate what it will do so the caller can plan I/O
   - done: https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/pull/10555 (@adriangb, @sunchao)
   - done: https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/pull/10158 (@zhuqi-lucas)

2. @adriangb / @HippoBaro: arrow-rs lets the decoder decode a row group incrementally, batch by batch, as its pages arrive
   - epic: https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/issues/11234 (@HippoBaro, @adriangb), 

3. @alamb / @adriangb / @Dandandan: make the I/O policy in DataFusion extensible, so the scan can choose between one request per row group, prefetch with a byte budget, or batch-granular fetch depending on the storage system
   - in progress: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/26387
   - in progress: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/23492
   - proof of concept: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/24086

issues.title: Account for retained sort-key capacity
issues.body:
Parent: #23393

Context: [PR comment](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/26074#discussion_r4198007007)

## Goal

Make partial group-ordering memory accounting include the retained allocation
for its `Vec<ScalarValue>` sort key.

## Invariant / contract

`GroupOrderingPartial::heap_size()` reports the retained heap allocations owned
by its state. For an in-progress state, this includes the sort-key vector's
allocated capacity and heap allocations owned by its initialized scalar
elements, each exactly once. It does not add an inline descriptor already
charged by `GroupOrdering::size()`.

## Tasks

- [ ] Replace the live-element-only sort-key accounting in
  `State::heap_size()` with capacity-aware `DFHeapSize` accounting, following
  the grouped `COUNT` accumulator's established approach.
- [ ] Add a deterministic test with spare `Vec<ScalarValue>` capacity and a
  heap-owning scalar, proving spare slots and initialized scalar payloads are
  accounted for without relying on allocator measurements.
- [ ] Preserve the existing ownership boundary: do not charge inline
  descriptors or allocations owned by other ordering state again.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An in-progress sort key with spare vector capacity reports that capacity
  even when the vector's live length is smaller.
- [ ] Heap allocations owned by initialized `ScalarValue`s remain included.
- [ ] Existing start/complete and ordering-state accounting behavior remains
  unchanged.

## Tests / verification

- Add or update the focused `GroupOrderingPartial` tests in
  `datafusion/physical-plan/src/aggregates/order/partial.rs`.
- Run `cargo test -p datafusion-physical-plan`.
- Run `./ci/scripts/doc_prettier_check.sh --write --allow-dirty` for this
  Markdown change.

## Dependencies / blockers

Keep the descriptor accounting established by the `GroupOrdering` owner
separate from this retained-capacity fix.

issues.title: EPIC: Separate optimizer rules from correctness transformation rules
issues.body:
Motivated by [this dicussion][epic-discussion].

DataFusion's physical optimizer currently mixes

1. Transformations required to make a plan executable (e.g. [`EnsureRequirements`][EnsureRequirements])
2. Optimizations intended to make it faster.

There are also several implicit assumptions that built-in rules make, such as:

- [`WindowTopN`][WindowTopN] assumes filters have no embedded projections  (see #21596).
- [`JoinSelection`][JoinSelection] assumes join inputs can still be swapped. Running it after post-optimization filter pushdown creates dynamic filters can violate that assumption and cause an internal planning error (see #26106).

Correctness depends on carefully ordering rules around implicit distribution and ordering enforcements, and on assumptions about what earlier rules have produced.

This makes rules difficult to understand, compose, and extend as rewrites can invalidate requirements, miss optimization opportunities, or undo one another's work. This can also lead to redundancy (e.g multiple repeated passes in the optimizer like in #25355)

### 
The goal of this epic is:
1. to separate correctness transformations from performance optimizations (perhaps by mirroring the logical [analyzer][AnalyzerRule]/[optimizer][OptimizerRule])
2. Remove as many implicit assumptions as possible

## Proposed work (outline)

- Define the correctness/optimization boundary and classify the existing rules (see #26171)
- Migrate rules to preserve validity, including rules currently placed before enforcement.

issues.title: Expressions evaluated in the Parquet scan lose field metadata (extension types) of columns replaced with literals
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

When a Parquet table has field metadata in its schema, such as an Arrow extension type (`ARROW:extension:name`), expressions evaluated inside the Parquet scan can see the column without that metadata. Expressions that read the field metadata of their arguments then see an empty map.

For example, `arrow_metadata(u)` returns `{}` for a Parquet column `u`, although the table schema has `ARROW:extension:name` on `u`. The same query over an in-memory table returns the metadata. Extension-aware UDFs that dispatch on the argument `Field` at execution time are affected the same way.

### To Reproduce

With `datafusion` 55.0.0 from PyPI. `skip_metadata=False` makes schema inference keep the field metadata; with the default `skip_metadata=True` the table schema has no field metadata at all, see #26851.

```python
import datafusion
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

# An extension type unknown to pyarrow, so that pyarrow keeps it as field metadata
field = pa.field("u", pa.binary(16), metadata={"ARROW:extension:name": "example.ext"})
table = pa.table({"u": pa.array([b"\x00" * 16], pa.binary(16))}, schema=pa.schema([field]))
pq.write_table(table, "ext.parquet")

ctx = datafusion.SessionContext()
ctx.register_parquet("t", "ext.parquet", skip_metadata=False)
print("table schema:", ctx.table("t").schema().field("u").metadata)

query = "SELECT arrow_metadata(u) AS m FROM t"
print("arrow_metadata(u):", ctx.sql(query).to_pylist())
print(ctx.sql(f"EXPLAIN {query}").to_pylist()[-1]["plan"])
```

Output:

```
table schema: {b'ARROW:extension:name': b'example.ext'}
arrow_metadata(u): [{'m': []}]
DataSourceExec: file_groups={1 group: [[.../ext.parquet]]}, projection=[arrow_metadata(u@0) as m], file_type=parquet
```

Controls on the same version:

| Query | `arrow_metadata(u)` |
|---|---|
| the same table registered with `register_record_batches` | `[('ARROW:extension:name', 'example.ext')]` |
| `SELECT u FROM t` on the Parquet table: field metadata of the returned batch | `{b'ARROW:extension:name': b'example.ext'}` |

So the scan itself returns `u` with its metadata. Only expressions pushed into `DataSourceExec` (`projection=[arrow_metadata(u@0) as m]`) see it without metadata.

**Cause.** The Parquet opener replaces column references with literals for partition columns and for columns that the file statistics prove constant (`min == max`). The literals are created without field metadata (`replace_columns_with_literals` in `datafusion/physical-expr-adapter/src/schema_rewriter.rs`, called from `datafusion/datasource-parquet/src/opener/mod.rs`). In the example, the file has one row, so `u` is constant and `arrow_metadata(u)` is evaluated on a literal without metadata.

The extension name is unknown to pyarrow (`example.ext`) only so that pyarrow keeps it as field metadata. A file written by DataFusion itself with an `arrow.uuid` column behaves the same way.

### Expected behavior

`arrow_metadata(u)` returns `{ARROW:extension:name: example.ext}`, as for the in-memory table: the scan produces fields with the metadata of the table schema.

### Additional context

Related: #26851 (schema inference drops extension types when `skip_metadata = true`) and #24721 (closed; projection field metadata lost when physical optimization removes a `ProjectionExec`).

### Willingness to contribute
I plan to contribute a fix for this bug independently

issues.title: Pruning of floating point Parquet columns is incorrect when `NaN` is present
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

This was mentioned in https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/15742#issuecomment-2815595171 and discussed in detail in https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/pull/221, but datafusion is over-aggressive in pruning floating point columns. The issue appears with predicates of the form `x [gt|lt] literal`. Consider a column consisting of `[1.0, 0.0, -1.0, NaN, -2.0]`, the max will be 1 and the min -2. A query like `select * from ... where x > 2` will return no rows because no chunk exists where `max > 2`.

### To Reproduce

```sql
> select * from 'parquet-testing/data/float16_nonzeros_and_nans.parquet' where x > arrow_cast(2.0, 'Float16');
+---+
| x |
+---+
+---+
0 row(s) fetched. 
```

### Expected behavior

The above query should return a single row containing `NaN`.

### Additional context

The Parquet community is considering changes to allow for `NaN` in statistics, with the currently favored approach being adding a new `ColumnOrder` to the specification. This will correct the issue above, but datafusion will need to check the `ColumnOrder` to know whether or not floating point statistics can be trusted.

Also note that if/when https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/pull/221 is merged, other predicates such as `isnan(x)` might be candidates for pruning, but that is an optimization.

issues.title: Run the sqllogictest corpus across a matrix of batch sizes
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

Almost all `sqllogictest` files run with a single `datafusion.execution.batch_size` (the default `8192`). Most `slt` tables are small, so nearly every operator sees one input batch per partition. Code paths that only run when the input is split across many batches are rarely exercised end to end: carrying state across batch boundaries, partial emits, coalescing, buffered join sides, and window frames that span batches.

#20919 showed that this gap hides real bugs. Building with `batch_size = 1` produced panics, internal assertion failures and wrong results, not just changed `EXPLAIN` output.

`# configMatrix:` (#24493) can already rerun a file across several values of a config key. Today only a few files sweep `batch_size` with it (`sort_merge_join_matrix.slt`, `piecewise_merge_join_matrix.slt`, `mark_join_matrix.slt`, `null_aware_multi_column.slt`, `piecewise_merge_join_nested_nulls.slt`). The rest of the corpus, covering aggregates, windows, sorts, unnest, limits, set operations and the other join files, runs at one batch size only.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Run the `slt` tests for all operators under a matrix of batch sizes, for example `1, 2, 7, 8192`. That would be a small size, a size that does not evenly divide typical row counts, and the default.

A possible shape:

1. Add a runner option, e.g. `--batch-sizes 1,2,7,8192`, that runs every file once per value. It would reuse the `configMatrix` machinery, so failures are reported with the combination that produced them. No per-file directive would be needed.
2. For non-default sizes, check only what does not depend on batch size:
   - Skip `EXPLAIN` records, since plans can change with batch size.
   - Compare results without regard to row order unless the query has an `ORDER BY`.
   - Give in-file `SET datafusion.execution.batch_size` precedence, or skip those files for the sweep.
3. Run the sweep in CI, either in the extended-tests job or nightly, so it does not slow down the main `sqllogictest` run.
4. Fix or file the failures it finds, then make the sweep required.

The default run stays as it is today and still checks plans and exact output.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- **Add `# configMatrix: datafusion.execution.batch_size=...` to each file.** This works with the existing runner, but it means editing about 600 `.slt` / `.slt.part` files. About 170 of them contain `EXPLAIN`, so they would first need to be split into a plan file and a matrix file. It also relies on every new file opting in.
- **Change the default `batch_size` only in the `slt` test context.** That tests one other value instead of several, and it changes the expected output of every `EXPLAIN` that prints the batch size.
- **Fuzz tests per operator.** These are useful, but they cover only the operators someone writes a fuzzer for and none of the SQL-level shapes in the corpus.

### Additional context

- #20919: crashes and wrong results with `batch_size = 1`
- #24390 / #24493: `configMatrix` support for `slt`
- #26152: a similar proposal to run the corpus under an alternative optimizer pipeline using the same machinery

issues.title: Let the data source veto `ExpressionPlacement::MoveTowardsLeafNodes` per function
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

This is a trade-off item, not a bug report.

`ExpressionPlacement` decides whether the leaf rules pull an expression out of a filter, a sort, a limit, an aggregate or a join, and push it down into the scan. The value comes from `ScalarUDFImpl::placement` in `datafusion/expr/src/udf.rs`, so it is a global constant of the function. Whether the push is a win depends on the data source.

https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/25036 and https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/25025 make the case for `bit_length`, `octet_length` and `array_length`. On Vortex the win is large: the source answers `octet_length("URL")` from its layout and never loads the string bytes. ClickBench Q29 is the example in the issue:

```sql
SELECT "CounterID", AVG(OCTET_LENGTH("URL")) AS l, COUNT(*) AS c
FROM hits WHERE "URL" <> '' GROUP BY "CounterID" HAVING COUNT(*) > 100000
ORDER BY l DESC LIMIT 25;
```

On Parquet the same mark has a different effect. The push moves the function below every filter in the plan, so it runs on every row of the scan instead of on the rows that survive the filter. Parquet has to decode the string to measure it, so nothing is saved. The physical guard, `would_duplicate_costly_exprs` in `datafusion/datasource/src/file_scan_config/mod.rs`, only refuses the merge when an expression is referenced more than one time. A single reference merges into the scan.

The same tension appears with `get_field`, which is already `MoveTowardsLeafNodes`. https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/14540 shows the plan it produces: `get_field` on both struct columns lands below the date filter. For a Parquet scan that absorbs the projection this is right, because the scan then reads one leaf instead of the whole struct. For a memory table, or for any source that cannot absorb the projection, the filter should run first.

The review of PR 25025 also found a concrete gap inside the mark itself. `array_length(arr, dim)` with a non-literal `dim` does a per-row traversal that depends on `dim`, so it is not cheap. `get_field` already guards this case: its `placement` returns `KeepInPlace` unless every key argument is a literal (`datafusion/functions/src/core/getfield.rs`). `array_length` needs the same guard. The reviewer's test was `SELECT x, x AS x2 FROM (SELECT array_length(column1, column2) AS x FROM t)`, which merges into one `ProjectionExec` holding `array_length(column1, column2)` two times.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Let the source say no.

Add a hook that the leaf rules consult before they push an expression into a scan, in the same spirit as `TableProvider::supports_filters_pushdown`. A sketch:

```rust
/// Which of `exprs` this source wants pushed into the scan.
/// Default: accept every expression the planner offers.
fn supports_leaf_expressions(
    &self,
    exprs: &[&Expr],
) -> Result<Vec<ExpressionPushdown>> { ... }
```

`ExpressionPushdown` needs at least two values, "absorb it" and "leave it above me". The hook belongs on `TableProvider`, and on `FileSource` for the file formats, so a Parquet source and a Vortex source can answer differently for `octet_length`.

With the hook in place, `ScalarUDFImpl::placement` states what the expression *can* be, and the source states what it *should* be for that scan. No global constant has to be right for every source.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

**A config option per function.** It does not help: one query can read a Parquet table and a Vortex table.

**A cost model on `ExpressionPlacement`.** A number instead of four buckets. The number that decides this case is the cost of the function *at that source*, plus the selectivity of the filters it is pushed below. Neither is available at planning time.

**Leave the placement global and rely on the physical guard.** `would_duplicate_costly_exprs` already blocks a merge when an expression is referenced more than one time. It does not block the single-reference case, which is the case in Q29, and it runs after the logical rules have already moved the expression below the filters.

### Additional context

The hook has to avoid the problem that https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/19929 reports for `supports_filters_pushdown`. That method is called without the filters that a previous optimizer pass already pushed, so a provider whose answer depends on what it already holds gives a wrong answer on the second pass. A leaf expression hook is called from a rule that runs to a fixed point, so it will be called more than one time on the same plan. It must receive the expressions the scan already absorbed, and the answer must be stable when the rule asks again.

Related:

- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/25025
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/25036
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/14540
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/19929

Tracked in the leaf-pushdown EPIC: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/25459

issues.title: Flatter representation of deeply nested `AND` / `OR` Expressions
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

DataFusion represents arbitrary binary Operator trees like 
```sql
(a OR (b OR (c OR (d OR ...)))
```

Using a binary tree structure called `BinaryExpr`:

https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/2da88876f6e764ca3052c92b9d1783929d13d7bf/datafusion/expr/src/expr.rs#L770-L779

There are also many places in the codebase where recursive algorithms are used to walk over Expr trees, 

An example of this is `Treenode::apply`: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/0838a4ddb902535b0e95a1c5a254be7e9c7fe9bf/datafusion/common/src/tree_node.rs#L196-L209


The stack depth is a function of the nesting depth of the expression, which means that

> [!IMPORTANT]
> In some cases processing deeply nested expressions can lean to a stack overflow (and thus a process `abort`)

This shows up in practice from Machine-generated SQL/filters with thousands of OR/AND terms (e.g. IN lists rewritten to OR, or large predicate pushdown

This representation has served us quite well, but we do have several mitigations

1. [`recursive` crate](https://crates.io/crates/recursive) + recursive_protection feature (segmented stack growth)

The primary mitigation. Recursive TreeNode drivers are annotated `#[cfg_attr(feature = "recursive_protection", recursive::recursive)]`, which uses the recursive crate  to grow the stack on the heap when it runs low, instead of overflowing. See the TreeNode walkers (6 sites — apply/transform_down/transform_up/rewrite/etc.): https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/0838a4ddb902535b0e95a1c5a254be7e9c7fe9bf/datafusion/common/src/tree_node.rs#L196-L209

2. SQL parser recursion limit (bounded recursion → error, not crash)

The [sqlparser crate ](https://crates.io/crates/sqlparser) itself caps nesting depth (default 50) and returns RecursionLimitExceeded rather than overflowing the stack.

3. Explicit-stack (iterative) SQL→Expr conversion
- See issue #1444

We also hit this a bunch when converting a [sqlparser](https://crates.io/crates/sqlparser) binary-operator tree into `Expr` and have a stack based conversion approach (see https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/0838a4ddb902535b0e95a1c5a254be7e9c7fe9bf/datafusion/sql/src/expr/mod.rs#L76-L120)

4. Out-of-line match arms in the expression simplifier

Large match arms are extracted into separate functions specifically to shrink per-frame stack usage and avoid overflow during simplification.

- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/0838a4ddb902535b0e95a1c5a254be7e9c7fe9bf/datafusion/optimizer/src/simplify_expressions/expr_simplifier.rs#L2335-L2341 


Recently people seem to be hitting recursion limits again and trying to put in patches, such as 
* https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/23198  from @mdashti
* https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/22943 from @nathanb

### Describe the solution you'd like

I would like a more fool proof way to avoid stack overflow issues



### Describe alternatives you've considered

## Option 1: n-ary expressions

The approach taken by DuckDb Mysql and Postgres is to represent `AND` and `OR` as n-ary rather than binary (2)

So that would be something like this (could also have an enum for And/Or)
```rust
enum ConjunctionType { And, Or }
/// AND/OR of some number of expressions
struct Conjunction {
  conjunction_type: ConjunctionType,
  /// Logically `exprs[0] AND (exprs[1] AND (exprs[2] AND ...`
  exprs : Vec<Expr>.
}
```

And then  
```rust
/// extend the Expr enum
enum Expr { 
  ...
  // AND
  Conjunction(Conjunction),
 ...
}
```

### Examples:

DuckDB uses ConjunctionExpression: https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/b8a06e4a22672e254cd0baa68a3dbed2eb51c56e/src/include/duckdb/parser/expression/conjunction_expression.hpp#L17-L27

Postrgres uses BoolExpr https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/REL_17_0/src/include/nodes/primnodes.h#L929-L942

Mysql uses [`Item_cond_and` / `Item_cond_or`](https://github.com/mysql/mysql-server/blob/mysql-8.0.40/sql/item_cmpfunc.h#L2711-L2768)  (based on [Item_cond base which stores args as a  List<Item> list](https://github.com/mysql/mysql-server/blob/mysql-8.0.40/sql/item_cmpfunc.h#L2421-L2447);

### Cons
This would be a major downstream API change 
Also unless we removed Operator::And / Operator::Or we would potentially have multiple ways to express the same logical expression


## Keep Binary Expr, have some sort of "balance" operation
Another approach taken by spark is to use Binary expressions: https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/fa33ea000a0bda9e5a3fa1af98e8e85b8cc5e4d4/sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/predicates.scala#L828

[`buildBalancedPredicate`](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/fa33ea000a0bda9e5a3fa1af98e8e85b8cc5e4d4/sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/predicates.scala#L160-L184) rebuilds a predicate list into a height-balanced tree in

issues.title: [EPIC] Variant on DataFusion
issues.body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

OpenSearch is adding a Variant field type to its Parquet-backed indices. The query engine is DataFusion, the writer and Variant kernels are arrow-rs, and the SQL functions are `datafusion-contrib/datafusion-variant`. Files mix shredded and unshredded layouts within one table, and the same table is read by Spark.

This epic lists the core hooks that work still needs, following the split in #16116: generic extension points in core, Variant-specific implementations in the crate. It sits under #16116 and #21308. Items already tracked elsewhere are linked rather than restated; the new issues are the ones marked **new**.

Spelling the type in SQL (section 6) already has issues filed on DF:
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/21144
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/21626
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/20755

They are linked here so the epic covers the whole core surface Variant needs.

### Describe the solution you'd like

#### 1. Read only the leaves a UDF needs

`variant_get(v, '$.x')` reads and decodes the whole Variant group because the Parquet planner only trusts `get_field`. Two PRs address this: #25013 (two hooks on `ScalarUDFImpl`) and draft #26282 (`NestedInputAccess` capability, also used by `get_field`, with row group and page pruning on the declared leaves). Our requirement for whichever shape lands: a function must be able to require more than one leaf for one argument (the typed leaf and the `value` fallback leaf), and pruning must keep any container that holds a fallback row. #26282 does both.

- [ ] Review #25013 / #26282 against shredded and unshredded test data and help converge on one shape
- [ ] Row group and page pruning on a declared leaf, with the fallback guard: #20871. #26282 includes it; if the work is split, this is the successor to #25013
- [ ] `datafusion-variant`: implement the capability for `variant_get` once it lands

#### 2. Keep the extension tag through planning

A Variant is a struct whose field metadata carries `ARROW:extension:name = arrow.parquet.variant`. Two core paths drop it, after which `variant_get` sees a plain struct and rejects the column.

- [ ] **new** Parquet schema inference clears all field metadata before `Schema::try_merge` when `skip_metadata = true` (the default, [`config.rs#L1343`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/common/src/config.rs#L1343)), so any `ListingTable` over more than one file loses the tag. The drop is [`clear_metadata`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/datasource-parquet/src/file_format.rs#L259-L272) in `datasource-parquet/src/file_format.rs`: every top-level `Field` is rebuilt `with_metadata(Metadata::new())`, which is exactly where the Variant tag lives. It is called from [`ParquetFormat::infer_schema`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/datasource-parquet/src/file_format.rs#L502-L506). Reproduced on 54. Proposed fix: keep the `ARROW:extension:*` keys recursively and drop the rest; the extension keys are the type's identity, not writer annotation.
- [ ] `CASE` / `COALESCE` build the output `Field` from the `DataType` alone: #24860 (reported on `geoarrow.wkb`, same mechanism). Drop sites:
  - `COALESCE`: [`CoalesceFunc::return_field_from_args`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/functions/src/core/coalesce.rs#L79-L90) takes `data_type()` and `is_nullable()` from the argument fields and returns `Field::new(name, return_type, nullable)`; the argument fields' metadata is never read.
  - `CASE`, logical plan: [`ExprSchemable::to_field`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/expr/src/expr_schema.rs#L707-L719) puts `Expr::Case` in the catch-all arm that returns `Field::new(name, get_type()?, nullable()?)` with no metadata.
  - `CASE`, physical plan: `CaseExpr` ([`case.rs#L1259`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/physical-expr/src/expressions/case.rs#L1259)) does not override `return_field`, so it inherits the [`PhysicalExpr::return_field` default](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/physical-expr-common/src/physical_expr.rs#L90-L96), which is again `Field::new(name, data_type()?, nullable()?)`.

#### 3. Tables that mix shredded and unshredded files

When one file stores `v` as `Struct<metadata, value>` and another as `Struct<metadata, value, typed_value: Struct<x: Int64>>`, the merged table schema has `typed_value`, and the default adapter null-fills it for the unshredded file. The fill never touches the files; it is an in-memory rewrite of the read expression, done once per file at open, in `DefaultPhysicalExprAdapter` (`physical-expr-adapter/src/schema_rewriter.rs`):

- Reading `v` whole: [`rewrite_column`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/physical-expr-adapter/src/schema_rewriter.rs#L752-L756) sees the file field differs from the table field and wraps the column in a `CastExpr` from the file struct to the table struct; the arrow struct cast adds `typed_value` as an all-null child at batch time.
- Reading `v['typed_value']` from a file that lacks it: [`try_rewrite_struct_field_access`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/physical-expr-adapter/src/schema_rewriter.rs#L670-L674) replaces the access with a null `Literal`; [`try_narrow_struct_cast`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/physical-expr-adapter/src/schema_rewriter.rs#L518-L530) does the same when the access goes through an adapter-inserted cast.
- The batch path applies the same rewrite to every `RecordBatch`: [`BatchAdapter::adapt_batch`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/physical-expr-adapter/src/schema_rewriter.rs#L924).

For an ordinary struct that is correct. For Variant the shredding spec makes `value = object, typed_value = null` an invalid row, so a compliant reader returns NULL for every field of every row of that file, silently. Reproduced: a two-file table returned 0 of 1024 unshredded rows. Files shredded on different keys fail differently, at open, with `target field is non-nullable but missing from source`, raised from the same place ([`rewrite_column`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/physical-expr-adapter/src/schema_rewriter.rs#L709-L714)).

The constraint we would like core to hold: a file is read in its own layout and reconstructed, never null-filled into a layout it does not have. Two ways to satisfy it: per-file `required_fields` answers (#26282 evaluates them against each file's schema at open, but states that "adapter-inserted struct casts are handled as before", so it narrows the read without removing the cast; whether `variant_get` then sees the file struct or the cast struct is to be confirmed), or a hook for a registered extension type to supply its own per-file adaptation, which satisfies the constraint by construction. The Variant adapter itself would live in the crate. Named earlier on #16116 (2025-07-15) and #22908 (2026-09-08).

- [ ] **new** Per-file adaptation for extension types, so an unshredded file is never null-filled into the shredded layout: per-file `required_fields` answers (#26282) or an extension-type adapter hook, with the Variant adapter in the crate

#### 4. Statistics the optimizer can use

`ColumnStatistics` is flat, so a nested leaf (shredded or not) and any UDF output have no planner statistics. Two designs are open for the UDF half and one has to be picked; #26282 adds a container-level `output_statistics` for pruning, which is a third data point.

- [ ] Nested and extension-type leaves in `Statistics`: #20707
- [ ] UDF output statistics: `ScalarUDFImpl::output_statistics` (#21307) or `ExpressionAnalyzer` (#21122). We implement whichever is chosen; the crate half (typed-leaf min/max, fallback-leaf null count) is the same code either way.

#### 5. Variant value semantics

`GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT`, joins and `ORDER BY` on a Variant column are undefined today. Spark rejects all of them at analysis time: [`OrderUtils.isOrderable`](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/branch-4.1/sql/api/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/OrderUtils.scala#L28) returns `false` for `VariantType`, which fails `=`/`<` and join keys in [`BinaryComparison.checkInputDataTypes`](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/branch-4.1/sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/predicates.scala#L1051) (`DATATYPE_MISMATCH.INVALID_ORDERING_TYPE`), `ORDER BY` in [`CheckAnalysis`](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/branch-4.1/sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/analysis/CheckAnalysis.scala#L627-L630) (`EXPRESSION_TYPE_IS_NOT_ORDERABLE`), `GROUP BY` (`GROUP_EXPRESSION_TYPE_IS_NOT_ORDERABLE`), and set operations in [`CheckAnalysis`](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/branch-4.1/sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/analysis/CheckAnalysis.scala#L843-L848), where the comment reads "remove this type check once we support Variant ordering". DuckDB 1.5 allows them but does not document the rule ([Variant docs](https://duckdb.org/docs/1.5/sql/data_types/variant) cover storage, `variant_typeof`, extraction and Parquet only); probed on 1.5: `=`, `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT` and `ORDER BY` each apply a different rule (equal numbers of different width compare equal but group apart; `ORDER BY` is by inner type tag, so `7.0` sorts after `42`).

- [ ] **new, after design discussion** A canonical-bytes normalisation kernel in arrow-rs so equal values have equal bytes, and a `variant_normalize` function in the crate on top of it, so hashing operators work without each inventing a rule. For `ORDER BY` our lean is to refuse at plan time as Spark does. Issue to follow once the SQL semantics are written up.

#### 6. Spelling `VARIANT` in SQL

The generic machinery is merged: `ExtensionTypeRegistry` and `DFExtensionType` (#20312, DataFusion 54), `TypePlanner` (#20676, 54), and metadata-preserving `CAST` (#23169, 55.1.0 via backport #24875). What is missing is the Variant entries. Without them a Variant prints as raw struct bytes in `datafusion-cli`, and `CREATE TABLE t (v VARIANT)` or `CAST(x AS VARIANT)` cannot be planned. Spark 4.2 and DuckDB 1.5 both spell the type `VARIANT` in `CREATE TABLE` and `CAST`, so this is what lets a query written for them run unchanged.

- [ ] Register `arrow.parquet.variant` as a [`DFExtensionType`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/common/src/types/extension.rs#L72-L90): `storage_type()` fixes the struct shape, `create_array_formatter()` gives JSON display in place of raw struct bytes (as [`DFUuid`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/common/src/types/canonical_extensions/uuid.rs#L59) does), and the registry entry is the identity the other hooks key on instead of re-parsing `ARROW:extension:name` from field metadata. The one unticked box in #21144. Small; the natural first PR
- [ ] Map the SQL name `VARIANT` to that type via `TypePlanner`: #21626, same shape as UUID and JSON. [`convert_data_type_to_field`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/sql/src/planner.rs#L672-L676) asks [`TypePlanner::plan_type_field`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/350ca76505c9513d16e7dd9910bcd9bde2c911ed/datafusion/expr/src/planner.rs#L516-L524) first; the Variant planner returns a `FieldRef` whose `DataType` is the Variant struct and whose metadata carries `ARROW:extension:name = arrow.parquet.variant`, taken from the `DFExtensionType` above. There is no `DataType::Variant`; the type is struct plus tag. The crate-side registration goes with it
- [ ] Pluggable cast resolution to and from extension types (`CAST(x AS VARIANT)`, `v::INT`): #20755, after the registration lands and a maintainer design. Not on our critical path

#### Adjacent, in arrow-rs

- [ ] The Parquet writer omits `specification_version` from the `VARIANT` logical type (`LogicalType::variant(None)` in `logical_type_for_struct`), although the Parquet spec requires the version in the declaration. Spark 4.1 only accepts version 1 and rejects the file with `PARQUET_TYPE_NOT_RECOGNIZED`; arrow-rs itself reads the file fine, so the gap only shows cross-engine. One-line fix: apache/arrow-rs#11917

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Keeping all of this inside OpenSearch (a fork of the Parquet reader and a private `variant_get`). Rejected: every hook above is generic to extension types, and the mixed-layout and statistics problems are hit by any Variant reader on DataFusion, not just ours.

### Additional context

Compatibility target for the crate work is Spark 4.2.0 (datafusion-variant#69). We build against DataFusion 54 today and are moving to 55 / arrow-rs 59, which the crate requires.

Open questions for maintainers:

1. Are items 2 and 3 accepted as core concerns (neither mentions Variant), with the Variant adapter shipped from the crate?
2. For item 1, which shape: #25013, #26282, or a merge of the two?
3. For item 4, #21307 or #21122?

issues.title: Three slow tests set the length of the extended and hash-collision CI jobs
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge?

Two merge-queue jobs spend most of their test time waiting on one or two slow tests, while every other test finished long before:

| Job | Runner | Test binary time | Other tests done by | Slow tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cargo test 'extended_tests'` | 32 vCPU | 229–238 s | 62–73 s | `leaf_pushdown_fuzz_extended` 229–238 s, `null_aware_join_matches_reference` 179–188 s |
| `cargo test hash collisions` | 16 vCPU | 118–122 s (physical-plan unit tests) | 24–25 s | both cases of `clustered_keys_match_hash_grouping_across_batches_and_emits`, 117–123 s |

These are from six merge-queue runs between Oct 24 and Oct 26. One Oct 24 run was faster overall (161 s and 132 s for the two extended tests) with the same shape.

Why each test is slow:

- `leaf_pushdown_fuzz_extended` runs 5,000 in-memory cases and then 1,000 Parquet cases, one after another (`datafusion/core/tests/fuzz_cases/leaf_pushdown_fuzz.rs`, the loop in `run` and the test at the bottom).
- `null_aware_join_matches_reference` builds 120 sessions (20 seeds × 2 `target_partitions` × 3 batch sizes) and runs every query and its reference query in each one (`datafusion/core/tests/fuzz_cases/null_aware_join_fuzz.rs`). The reference result should be the same for every config, but it is recomputed for each.
- `clustered_keys_match_hash_grouping_across_batches_and_emits` compares `GroupValuesClustered` with `GroupValuesColumn` over every key type, nullability, sort direction, 6 batch sizes and 4 emit limits. `GroupValuesClustered` does no hashing, so forcing hash collisions only slows down the `GroupValuesColumn` reference, and the hash-collision job gets no extra coverage of the code under test.

### Describe the solution you'd like

- `leaf_pushdown_fuzz_extended`: run the seeds in a few concurrent chunks. The report already counts failures across all seeds and keeps the first one, so the chunks' results can be merged into the same report.
- `null_aware_join_matches_reference`: compute each reference once per seed and compare every config against it, as #26644 did for the join fuzz test.
- `clustered_keys_match_hash_grouping_across_batches_and_emits`: skip it under `force_hash_collisions`, as #26594 did for another test.

Estimated effect: the extended test binary drops from about 235 s to about 70 s, and the physical-plan unit tests in the hash-collision job from about 120 s to about 25 s. The merge queue ran 198 times in the last week, so this frees about 165 s of a 32-vCPU runner and 95 s of a 16-vCPU runner per run, roughly 110 vCPU-minutes per run. The microbenchmark job (about 13 minutes) still decides how long a merge group takes, so this saves runner time, not queue time.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- Lower the case counts (fewer seeds, a smaller grid). Simpler, but it drops coverage; chunking and reusing the reference keep every case.
- For the clustered test, a smaller grid would also help the regular `cargo test` job, where these two cases are the last physical-plan unit tests to finish (40 s). That changes what the test covers, so it is a call for the test's author.

### Additional context

Part of #13813.

### Willingness to contribute

I'm not planning to work on this myself, so anyone is welcome to pick it up. The three tests are independent, so they can also go in separate PRs. Feel free to ping me with questions or when you'd like a review.

issues.title: [DISCUSSION] 2026 Q4 Roadmap
issues.body:
- part of https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/21036
-  Follow on to https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/22882

As I have said before, it is still mind boggling 🤯  to me that DataFusion has gotten so far without central planning authority, but the decentralized model has served us (very) well and I don't think we need to change. However, [the rise of AI generated code](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/26257), especially in the last few months, has been challenging this model as it is so easy to generate changes, I think the collective attention of the community has been overwhelmed and we are thrashing. See for example these discussions
- #23839 from @jayzhan211 
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/discussions/24413 from @Jefffrey 
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/24510
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/25973 from @2010YOUY01 

What I suggest is that  a few maintainers agree to help one or more projects along and then prioritize reviews of related PRs. 

As always, I expect DataFusion priorities to be driven by what the maintainers want to help drive to completion. However, I also personally think the community would benefit from some  agreement  on higher level  "Light House" areas to focus our collective attention on before we wade into the sea of PRs. Since I am just one voice, I don't get to choose what everyone else works on, but I here are some of my suggestions to get the conversation flowing.


# Tier 1: Correctness
What: Ensure answers are always correct
Goal: Have DataFusion be the standard to compare against
Tracking Epic:
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/26672

# Tier 1: Performance (TBD)
I think it would be great to agree on or two areas to really focus and improve performance. My suggestion is either Parquet IO Patterns and Join benchmark performance, but I think there are other compelling areas to 


Some options:

### Performance Option: Parquet IO patterns
What: Make the I/O pattern of Parquet scans deliberate and configurable (one request per row group, bounded prefetch, or batch-granular fetch) instead of a hard coded trade-off between latency and memory
Goal: lower time to first batch and peak memory per partition, overlap I/O with decode, and let the scan adapt to the storage system (object store vs local SSD)
Recent Epics:
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/26682

### Performance Option: Join Benchmark Performance
What: Improve performance in Join heavy benchmarks
Goal: ensure we keep DataFusion at the top of benchmarks (especially join heavy ones), 
Recent Epics:
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/26661
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/26169

### Performance Option: Filter Pushdown
What: Enable Parquet filter pushdown (late materialization) by default and finish the logical filter / leaf expression pushdown work
Goal: evaluate filters as early as possible (during the scan where it helps) without performance regressions
Recent Epics:
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/22883
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/20324
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/25459
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/15512

### Performance Option: Nested and Semi-structured Data 
What: Improve struct field access, nested schema pruning and Variant support in the Parquet scan
Goal: make queries over nested columns as efficient as over flat ones
Recent Epics:
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/24119
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/21308
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/26517


Other potential projects we might want to rally around:
- Spilling Joins: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/24768
- blocked / chunked memory in hash aggregation: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/24704
- Optimize range partitioning for joins and distributed pipelines: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/25421
- Subplan materialization: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/22676
- Adaptive predicate evaluation: https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/22883


# Things I personally plan to deemphasize
* Seemingly random improvements to random parts of the code, especially if it [isn't from a DataFusion user](https://andrew.nerdnetworks.org/blog/2026/10/19/my-plan-for-reviewing-prs-in-open-source-projects-in-the-age-of-ai/) or from a [Prolific Author](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pulls?q=is%3Apr+state%3Aopen+label%3A%22Prolific+Author%22)

issues.title: Partial aggregate state reaches the final aggregate without a memory reservation (median, array_agg)
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

For aggregates whose state holds every input value, such as `median`, `percentile_cont` and `array_agg`, the state moves from the partial aggregate to the final aggregate without a memory reservation. The partial aggregate emits its whole state as one batch, then its stream ends and releases its reservation. The final aggregate reserves memory only after it has merged a batch. In between, states as large as the input are held unreserved, so a plan with more than one partition uses far more memory than the pool allows.

### To Reproduce

Run each query in its own `datafusion-cli` process (`/usr/bin/time -l` is macOS; use `-v` on Linux):

```sh
# Query 1
/usr/bin/time -l datafusion-cli -m 300m \
  -c "SET datafusion.execution.target_partitions = 1;" \
  -c "SELECT median(v) FROM generate_series(1, 30000000) AS t(v);"

# Query 2
/usr/bin/time -l datafusion-cli -m 300m \
  -c "SET datafusion.execution.target_partitions = 4;" \
  -c "SELECT median(v) FROM generate_series(1, 30000000) AS t(v);"
```

### Expected behavior

| Query | Plan | Peak RSS, 6 runs each (300 MB limit) | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `AggregateExec: mode=Single` | 519 MB every run | (baseline) |
| 2 | `Partial` -> `Final` | 656 MB to 939 MB | About the same as Query 1: the extra memory is the partial states, which should be reserved while held |

Query 1 is above the limit for a separate reason: its value buffer reallocates into one twice its size before freeing the old one, the same shape as #25606.

### Additional context

- The partial `state()` moves all values into a single list value: [percentile_cont.rs#L469-L495](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/039c0b99d5b05e73ff5def029c0131b76b481c6f/datafusion/functions-aggregate/src/percentile_cont.rs#L469-L495).
- `AggregateStream` grows its reservation only after a batch has been aggregated: [aggregate_stream.rs#L407-L411](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/039c0b99d5b05e73ff5def029c0131b76b481c6f/datafusion/physical-plan/src/aggregates/aggregate_stream.rs#L407-L411).
- Counting allocations against reservations (the approach of #25651) at 10M rows, the final aggregate had 96 bytes reserved while 147 MB was allocated. `array_agg(s) ... GROUP BY v % 10` shows the same gap.
- One direction: the final aggregate reserves an incoming state batch before merging it, since the contract in `memory_pool/mod.rs` makes the operator that holds batches responsible for them.
- Related: #25851, #26701.

### Willingness to contribute

I'm not planning to fix this myself, so anyone is welcome to pick it up. Feel free to ping me with questions about the cause or when you'd like a review.

issues.title: [EPIC] Use blocked / chunked memory management in hash aggregation
issues.body:
Note: this issue consolidates and replaces https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/7065, which dates from 2023 and predates much of the discussion.

## What is going on (symptoms)

High-cardinality `GROUP BY` queries in DataFusion suffer from several challenges that look unrelated at first, but all trace back to the same root cause. The problems:

1. **Aggregation memory is held until the hash table is fully drained.** All group state is emitted as slices of one giant batch, so none of it is released until the last output batch. For a typical [two-stage aggregation][multi-phase], this shows up as ~2x peak memory: while the first stage drains its 1 GB of state, the final stage is simultaneously building its own ~1 GB (measured by @2010YOUY01 in https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/22712).

2. **Queries with more than 2 GiB of overall string data in group keys can crash outright.** All the bytes of `Utf8`/`Binary` group keys are interned into one contiguous buffer addressed by `i32` offsets; once more than 2 GiB of key bytes accumulate, the offsets overflow and the query fails with `offset overflow, buffer size > 2147483647`:
   - https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/23694 (reported by @maxburke)
   - https://github.com/apache/datafusion-comet/issues/4718 (report from Comet by @comphead)
   - https://github.com/apache/datafusion-comet/pull/4791 (workaround by @comphead)

3. **Downstream memory accounting is off / operators spill when they don't need to.** Each output batch reports the memory of the *entire* aggregation output via [`get_array_memory_size()`], which causes unnecessary spilling in operators such as [`RepartitionExec`] and [`TopK`]:
   - https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/22526 (reported by @ariel-miculas)
   - https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/9562 (reported by @alamb)

4. **The async runtime stalls when output begins.** Producing output for >500k groups block a tokio worker thread for hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, causing latency spikes for everything else on that thread:
   - https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/19906 (reported by @ahmed-mez)

5. **Potential copying performance.** As groups accumulate, internal buffers [repeatedly double in size and copy all existing data][vec-growth] (up to 2 copies per element on average), which is likely expensive and cache/TLB unfriendly and could in theory be avoided.
   - https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/11931 (reported by @Rachelint)


## What is causing the problem

Note you can read more about the current group state in the blog [Aggregating Millions of Groups Fast in Apache Arrow DataFusion 28.0.0](https://datafusion.apache.org/blog/2023/08/05/datafusion_fast_grouping/)

[`GroupedHashAggregateStream`] stores all per-group state in **single contiguous buffers that grow by doubling**:

- **Group keys** are stored by a [`GroupValues`] implementation (e.g. [`PrimitiveGroupValueBuilder`] or [`ByteGroupValueBuilder`]). The hash table itself only stores *group indexes* — `usize` offsets into these buffers.
- **Aggregate state** is stored by one [`GroupsAccumulator`] per aggregate expression (not per group). Each accumulator manages the state for *all* groups, typically as a single `Vec<T>` (plus a null buffer), again indexed by a single group index (a `usize`).

```text
                                         ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
                                         │┌────────────┐│   │┌────────────┐│   │┌────────────┐│
    ┌─────┐                              ││accumulator ││   ││accumulator ││   ││accumulator ││
    │  5  │                              ││     0      ││   ││     0      ││   ││     0      ││
    ├─────┤                              ││ ┌────────┐ ││   ││ ┌────────┐ ││   ││ ┌────────┐ ││
    │  9  │                              ││ │ state  │ ││   ││ │ state  │ ││   ││ │ state  │ ││
    ├─────┤                              ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││
    │     │                              ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││

    │  1  │                              ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││

    │     │                              ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││
    └─────┘                              ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││

                                         │└────────────┘│   │└────────────┘│   │└────────────┘│
    Hash Table                           └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘


stores "group indexes"                     There is one GroupsAccumulator per aggregate
which are indexes into                     (NOT PER GROUP). Internally, each
the state vectors                          GroupsAccumulator manages the state for
                                           multiple groups
```

This contiguous layout explains each symptom:

1. **Memory held until drained**: output is produced via [`EmitTo::All`]: at end of input, **all** groups are materialized into one giant `RecordBatch`, which is then [handed downstream as `batch.slice(..)` chunks of `batch_size` rows][emit-slice]. The slices share the giant batch's buffers, so no memory is freed until the last slice is dropped.
2. **Crash on wide string keys**: for `Utf8`/`Binary` group keys, [`ByteGroupValueBuilder<i32>`] stores all key bytes in a single contiguous buffer addressed by `i32` offsets, so accumulating more than 2 GiB of key bytes overflows.
3. **Spilling / accounting**: every slice of the giant batch reports the full underlying allocation to the memory accounting, not just its own rows.
4. **Runtime stall**: materializing all groups in a single [`EmitTo::All`] call is one large CPU-bound operation with no await point.
5. **Copying performance**: growing the contiguous buffers requires reallocating and copying all existing data.

## The high level solution sketch

The fix that everyone seems to agree on is to store group keys and accumulator state in **multiple blocks** instead of one contiguous `Vec`. This is the approach [used by DuckDB][duckdb-agg] and most other databases with buffer managers, which don't have the luxury of large contiguous arrays. It was [originally suggested for DataFusion by @yjshen in 2023][yjshen-suggestion].

At a high level, the idea is that:

- Blocks store some number of rows (most likely `target_batch_size`)
- Blocks are not resized; when a block fills up, a new block is allocated (which avoids copying and the growth is predictable and incremental)
- A group index becomes some form of `(block_id, offset)` rather than a single `group_idx`
- Emission now happens one block at a time (e.g. something like `EmitTo::NextBlock`), so memory is freed incrementally. The blocks now back individual output `RecordBatch`es (fixing the accounting).
- Since each block is capped at `target_batch_size` rows, they are far more likely to stay below 2 GiB of total string values (the `i32` offset limit), avoiding the string offset overflow.

The idea is illustrated here:
```text
                                         ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
                                         │┌────────────┐│   │┌────────────┐│
    ┌─────────┐                          ││accumulator ││   ││accumulator ││
    │  (0,5)  │                          ││    AGG     ││   ││    SUM     ││
    ├─────────┤                          ││ ┌────────┐ ││   ││ ┌────────┐ ││
    │  (1,3)  │                          ││ │ block  │ ││   ││ │ block  │ ││
    ├─────────┤                          ││ │   0    │ ││   ││ │   0    │ ││
    │         │                          ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││
    ├─────────┤                          ││ │        │ ││   ││ │        │ ││

    │         │                          ││            ││   ││            ││
    └─────────┘                          ││ ┌────────┐ ││   ││ ┌────────┐ ││

    Hash Table                           ││ │   1    │ ││   ││ │   1    │ ││

as (block_id, offset)                      fixed size blocks: a full block is
pairs into the block                       never resized; instead a new block
storage                                    is allocated as needed, and whole
                                           blocks can be emitted / freed
                                           one at a time
```


## Why this is hard to fix

The reason this is so hard to implement is that the entire API is designed around a single `usize` group index that is [assumed to be contiguous and directly addressable][group-index-contiguous]:

- [`GroupValues::intern`] assigns each distinct group key a dense index `0..n`, and the hash table stores those raw indexes.
- [`GroupsAccumulator::update_batch`] receives `group_indices: &[usize]` and `total_num_groups: usize`; implementations index their state `Vec`s directly with the group index and grow them with a single `resize(total_num_groups)`.
- [`EmitTo::First(n)`]: after emitting the first `n` groups, [every remaining group index is renumbered down by `n`][`EmitTo::First(n)`] — a notion that only makes sense when the state is one contiguous array.

For example [`GroupValues::intern`]:

```rust
pub trait GroupValues: Send {
    // Required methods
    fn intern(
        &mut self,
        cols: &[Arc<dyn Array>],
        groups: &mut Vec<usize>,   // <---- groups are identified by contiguous `usize`
    ) -> Result<(), DataFusionError>;

    ...
}
```

Because this assumption is spread across every [`GroupValues`] and [`GroupsAccumulator`] implementation — including user-defined aggregates and the FFI bindings — moving to a blocked `(block_id, offset)` index:
1. Potentially touches the whole ecosystem at once (aka is a massive change)
2. Likely involves an extra memory lookup in the **hottest** critical path: once to find the base pointer for the `block_id` and once to find the actual value within that block.

We have discussed ways to address both issues:
1. Incremental rollout: neither option found so far is great — supporting blocked *and* contiguous layouts in each implementation leads to the dual code paths and generics that made #15591 so complex, while switching the index semantics outright is a breaking change that is very hard to stage incrementally (see the discussion on https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/15591).
2. Different strategies for small and large aggregates: use direct indexing while the hash table is small (where the extra indirection would hurt most), and switch to two part `(block_id, offset)` indexes once the table grows past a threshold — at that point accesses are cache misses anyway, so the extra lookup matters less. See https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/15591#issuecomment-5333397682 and the earlier version of the same idea in https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/22712#issuecomment-4672476038.

## Past attempts and prototypes

There is a long and distinguished history of trying to address this problem:

| PR | Year | What it showed | Outcome |
|----|------|----------------|---------|
| https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/11758 | 2024 | Generate GroupByHash output in multiple `RecordBatch`es (@JasonLi-cn) | Closed unmerged |
| https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/11943 | 2024 | First sketch of blocked management (@Rachelint) | Closed, superseded by #15591; motivated the aggregation fuzz test framework (#12114) |
| https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/15591 | 2025 | Full blocked implementation (@Rachelint): `supports_blocked_groups` / `alter_block_size` trait additions, blocked [`PrimitiveGroupsAccumulator`] + [`GroupValuesPrimitive`] | Open. Extensive review concluded the dual-mode (blocked + contiguous) design is too complex, and some aggregates regress ~10% |
| https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/20964 | 2026 | `BatchedVec<T>` bench (@Dandandan): O(1) per-block emission is achievable in small steps | Closed (proof of concept) |
| https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/22712 | 2026 | PoC on refactored streams (@2010YOUY01): 10–16% faster at medium/high cardinality; memory curve becomes bell-shaped instead of monotonically growing; ClickBench Q5 +61% pending the skip-partial-aggregation fast path | Closed (proof of concept; demonstrated the #22710 refactor is necessary first) |
| https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/23274 | 2026 | `EmitTo::FirstBlock` as an API-only first step (@hhhizzz) | Closed: the API should follow the blocked physical layout rather than precede it |

One seemingly obvious alternative would be to use [`EmitTo::First(n)`] to incrementally emit data from the front of the state. However, this does not work either as it is *destructive*: it requires [shifting all remaining elements to the start of the buffers][take-n] and [renumbering every remaining group index][`EmitTo::First(n)`]. @ahmed-mez tried incremental emission with these mechanics in https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/19562 and measured it ~15x slower at high cardinality.


As part of https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/22710, @2010YOUY01 has been refactoring the monolithic [`GroupedHashAggregateStream`] into dedicated per-path streams, in large part to make changes like blocked state management feasible to implement and review. I (@alamb) thinks completing this refactor is a **prerequisite** for beginning the blocked state work in earnest: implementing it against the old multiplexed stream would be far more complex and would conflict with the refactoring itself.

The same blocked approach was also proposed independently by @alchemist51 in https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/19649, which includes an experiment (based on @Rachelint's #15591) where a high-cardinality query that fails with resource exhaustion in a 16 GB memory pool today completes once blocked state management is enabled.

An in-progress implementation for multi-column group-by (@rluvaton) using only `EmitTo::NextBlock` is being discussed on https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/15591. It is not yet a PR, but the work seems to be on the [`add-blocks-impl` branch](https://github.com/rluvaton/datafusion/tree/add-blocks-impl) of their fork.

A complementary approach that reduces partial-stage state without changing these traits is cache-efficient (morsel-driven) partial aggregation, proposed by @Dandandan:
- https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/20773
